listenings.text: Right, welcome, everyone. Three quick tips before we start. First, almost all of my students worry about the speaking test, and honestly, it's far less scary than you think. It's a conversation with a real person, not a machine. Second, take a mock test in the first week, not the last. At the beginning, the format is the hardest part, and the more you know it, the better you'll do. And third, find out the cutoff score for your university or your visa. If they ask for a band score of seven, aim slightly higher, seven and a half. That way a bad day won't ruin your plans.

When we hire, a certificate is useful, but it's not the whole story. A good TOEIC score tells me that the candidate can read and understand English at a certain level. That's important. But for most positions, the interview is far more important than the certificate. I want to see how people speak, how they react to a question they didn't expect. Last year we had two candidates for the same job. One had a slightly higher score. The other was much better in the interview: relaxed, natural, she asked us questions. She got the job. So my advice is simple. Get the certificate, but don't stop practicing conversation.

Every semester I meet students who booked the most expensive test too early. They pay a lot, they're not ready, and they have to take it again. What a waste. Here's what I recommend. Start with a cheaper online test. It won't open every door, but it tells you your level in about an hour. Then weigh up your options. Do you need it for a university? For a job? For a visa? And give yourself time. The more time you give yourself to prepare, the better your result will be. Two or three months is usually far better than two or three weeks.

reading.rtitle: Five Tests, Five Doors: A Short Guide
paras: There is no single best English test. There are five popular ones, and each was built for a different door. The TOEFL is by far the most common choice for universities in the United States, and it assesses all four skills: listening, reading, speaking and writing. The IELTS also tests the four skills, but it is much more popular in the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, and it is accepted for study, work and immigration. Your result is a band score from 0 to 9.

If your goal is a job, the TOEIC is worth a look. Many employers, especially large companies, use it to assess English for the workplace. The classic TOEIC tests only listening and reading, so it is not nearly as complete as the TOEFL or the IELTS, and companies that need speaking usually ask for a separate test or an interview. Cambridge exams, like C1 Advanced, are different in one important way: the certificate does not expire, while most other results are valid for only two years.

Finally, the Duolingo English Test is far more affordable than the others, and you can take it online, at home, in about one hour. More and more universities accept it, although it is still less common among employers. For many people, it is a worthwhile first step: a cheap way to check their level before they weigh up the bigger tests. Whatever you choose, take at least one mock test first. The more you know the format, the calmer you will feel, and the better your score will be.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- B2 reading, written for this lesson. Prices, formats and validity rules change: always check the official website of each test.
